paras: The lynching of Joseph Daroche took place in Bodie, California, at about 1 a.m. on January 17, 1881, when a vigilance committee took him from the town jail and hanged him where he was accused of shooting the miner Thomas H. Treloar three days earlier. It followed his escape, recapture and a preliminary examination, and some 500 men reportedly watched. Wire dispatches carried the story nationally under headlines such as "Judge Lynch at Bodie," and Nevada papers followed the town's quarrel over vigilante rule for weeks.

According to a Bodie dispatch of January 14, Treloar was shot through the head at about 2 a.m. by "a Frenchman named De Roche" after a ball at which Treloar's wife had danced with De Roche against her husband's orders. De Roche was arrested and jailed, but Deputy Sheriff Joseph Farnsworth, claiming that vigilantes meant to hang the prisoner, took him handcuffed to his own boarding-house, where he disappeared while Farnsworth slept.

The Vigilance Committee, armed with shotguns, searched houses and the jail until daylight and, a dispatch said, would have hanged Farnsworth had he been found. A coroner's jury found Treloar's death a willful and premeditated murder by Deroche, censured Deputy Sheriff Kirgan and called Farnsworth criminally careless, and Farnsworth fled to Carson, where he was arrested.

Daroche was captured on Sunday morning, January 16, at a wood ranch six miles from Bodie, and there was a "strong disposition" to lynch him on arrival. After speeches for and against lynching, he was given a preliminary examination before Justice Newman. After dark a vigilance committee known as "The Bodie 601" was organized, and at about 1 a.m. it took him from the jail to the scene of the shooting and hanged him "exactly over the spot where it occurred." The dispatch said "Fully 500 men" watched; a separate dispatch in the Omaha Bee said a "body of citizens" hanged him to a tree at the spot.

Farnsworth was freed at Carson when word of the lynching arrived, and the Bodie Free Press demanded a complete reorganization of the police force. Treloar's widow was later reported "ordered to leave by the Vigilantes." No report of an inquest on Daroche, or of any charge against the vigilantes, appears in the coverage.

By February about ninety residents had formed a "Bodie Law and Order Association," pledging to oppose crime "by an individual or a mob" and to protect accused men from "a self-constituted hanging committee." A month later the Free Press, complaining of lax officers after a saloon shooting, held up "the one which salted DaRoche" as the kind of organization the town needed.

Coverage came entirely from white papers and rested on one Bodie dispatch of January 17, printed in full by the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and the Gold Hill Daily News. The Record-Union headed it "Judge Lynch at Bodie—Economical Trial and Punishment of a Murderer" and the Gold Hill News "Justice at Bodie," both repeating that no one was dissatisfied "except the gamblers and saloon men." Shorter versions ran in Los Angeles, Cheyenne, Washington and Dallas, the last as "A Murderer Lynched," while the Omaha Bee's own dispatch, "Stern Retribution," called the crime "unprovoked."

Weekly digests in Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Ohio and Louisiana cut the story to a sentence or two. The Gold Hill News mocked the Law and Order men and predicted that "601 goes right ahead," while the San Bernardino Times, quoted in New Jersey, listed the lynching among a week of Pacific-coast killings and urged juries to convict murderers. Apart from calling Daroche a Frenchman or French Canadian, no paper described the race of anyone involved.

The Carson Tribune, quoted by the Weekly Elko Independent, said vigilantes tracked the fugitive to Smith's Dump, about ten miles away, where two French Canadians were "strung up" and tortured until they revealed his hiding place. In that version the lawyer Pat Reddy asked the mob to leave him to the courts, and an informal jury trial was held instead. The Tribune had the particulars only "so far as we can learn"; the Bodie dispatch, placing the capture at a wood ranch and the hearing before Justice Newman, is the more direct source.

reader.title: Lynching of Joseph Daroche
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: An organized vigilance committee took an accused murderer from the Bodie jail and hanged him at the scene of the killing before a large crowd (A5, A8, A22).

A vigilance committee with no legal authority, 'The Bodie 601', took Daroche from jail and hanged him for the killing of Thomas H. Treloar after a preliminary examination, with no trial in a court (A5, A8, A22). Nothing in the coverage indicates the victim was Black; he was described as a Frenchman or French Canadian (A1, A23).

The Bodie wire dispatch (A4, A5, A8), the Omaha Bee's separate San Francisco dispatch (A11), the Carson Tribune account (A17) and later Nevada press (A22, A25) all agree that Bodie vigilantes hanged the accused, though they differ on how he was captured and tried.

record_check.dossier: 'Fully 500 men witnessed the execution' in every version that gives a number.
Race not stated; described as a Frenchman or French Canadian miner, formerly of Chicago. No indication the victim was Black.
A vigilance committee known as 'The Bodie 601'.
Seizure from jail and hanging; the 'killing' is the accused's own alleged killing of Treloar, not an act of the mob.

info: Hanged about 1 a.m. on January 17, 1881 (night of Jan. 16-17), after capture on Sunday, January 16; the killing of Treloar was about 2 a.m. Friday, January 14.
Bodie, at the spot where Treloar had been shot; taken from the Bodie jail.

Joseph Daroche (also printed De Roche, Deroche, Darchee, Darooche, Darroche, Doroche, De la Roche), described as a Frenchman or French Canadian miner, formerly of Chicago, with a wife and three children in Chicago.
Accused of shooting Thomas H. Treloar, a miner, through the head after Treloar objected to his dancing with Treloar's wife at a ball; a coroner's jury called it willful and premeditated murder.
A vigilance committee called 'The Bodie 601' (OCR 'Bodie Six Hundred and One'), organized after dark.
